title: Suites, SaaS, Open Source and Composable: The Platform Landscape in 2026
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/05-commerce-platform-landscape/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter. It is a contract, not a description: after the reconstruction the order of ideas was changed from the flow rubric (see decision_log) and the chapter was revised to match.

know: Seven platform categories and where each puts the integration work and the cost.
That most platforms are priced on the merchant's sales, with dated figures.
believe: A platform category moves integration work; it does not remove it.
can_do: Read a vendor's 2026 pitch as a layer to add or a move to make, and say who would carry the work afterwards.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or product manager who has inherited a platform and is about to sit through a replatforming pitch. The chapter is written at the level of Noor Visser in February 2027, before she had the vocabulary to answer 'what kind of platform are we on?'. Analysts and leaders who must read vendor decks and analyst charts get the reading guide.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 incidents and the names of the failure patterns, in outline (meet-kestrel-and-pine, where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong).

From journey-of-an-order: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, that a system is any software or outside service that takes part in handling an order, 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems that make and keep promises, Kestrel & Pine's seven systems in the order walk and thirteen in its landscape.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub, availability service, D2C, B2B.
From commerce-business-models: the business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group).
From boundaries-and-systems-of-record: bounded contexts, system of record, single writer, events and reconciliation, and the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
does_not_know: The category names and what separates them: hosted SaaS platform, enterprise suite, open source and fork, composable, headless, MACH, ERP-centered commerce, specialist layer, specialist group.
Deployment words: on-premises, platform-as-a-service, tenant, replatforming.
Pricing words: GMV as a pricing base, transaction fee, interchange, run-rate, trailing sales.
The layer acronyms as products one can buy: OMS, PIM, POS.
How to read a vendor's number (unit, date, definition) and a vendor's public record (revenue mix, strategic review, ownership).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two platforms with the same feature list, the reader names three operating-model differences to ask about before comparing features.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Two platforms both offer cart, catalog and checkout. What would you ask before comparing features?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Who runs hosting and upgrades; how the price moves with sales; who carries integration and what leaving costs.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a one-line description of a product, the reader places it in a category and says where the integration work lands.
acceptance_criteria.probe: One vendor sells a storefront, cart and checkout that it hosts for many merchants, with an app store. A second vendor sells cart and catalog services reachable only through an API, with no storefront. Using only this chapter: which kind of platform is each, and with each, where does the work of connecting it to a merchant's other systems land?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The first is a hosted SaaS platform: the integration work lands on the apps, webhooks and connectors the merchant installs. The second is a composable (headless, API-only) vendor: the integration work lands on the merchant, by design, who must also build or buy the storefront.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a platform's monthly list price, the reader says why it is not the cost and names the lines that move with sales.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A hosted platform quotes a merchant €2,300 a month. Using only this chapter: why is that figure not what the platform will cost, and what would you ask for before comparing it with another vendor's price?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The subscription is the smallest line; platforms are priced mainly on the merchant's sales and payments (payment fees, a transaction fee when another payment provider is used, a tier or percentage tied to GMV). Ask for the total paid in a year including those fees and what share of it is a percentage of sales.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal to replace a platform after an incident, the reader says what the chapter advises and who would carry the work after the move.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After a stock incident, a consultancy proposes that a merchant with stores, marketplaces and a small technology team replace its hosted platform with a composable set of separate products. Using only this chapter: what does the author advise, and who would carry the integration work after such a move?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Keep the platform and add the missing capability as a layer beside it (an order management system or availability service), because a move does not remove the integration work: with composable it lands on the merchant, whose team would have to build and run the joins. Choose by the team you have; composable per capability around a kept core at that stage.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a number from a vendor's deck, the reader asks for its unit, its date and its definition, and can name one way such a number misleads.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A vendor's presentation says '500+ customers' and '$100 billion GMV run-rate'. Using only this chapter: what would you ask about each number before comparing this vendor with another?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The unit, the date and the definition of each. A run-rate annualizes a recent period and is not a full year, and GMV is the value of orders through the platform, not the vendor's revenue; 'customers' may count shops, brands, enterprises or users, which differ by large factors.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader new to commerce meets no term in this chapter before it is explained, and every acronym is expanded on first use.

thesis.question: What kinds of platforms exist, who sells them, how they are priced and how the market changed up to 2026?
thesis.claim: The category of a commerce platform decides where the integration work and the cost land rather than whether they exist, so a merchant should choose by the work it can carry, and should read every 2026 pitch as a layer to add beside what it has, not a reason to move.
thesis.disputed_by: Feature comparisons and vendor claims that one category (composable, suite, hosted) is the modern answer for everyone.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that replatforms to escape integration work finds the same work on the other side, under a different owner and price.
thesis.how_why: Hosted platforms push variation to apps, suites keep integration inside one data model, open source moves hosting and upgrades to the merchant and composable moves integration to the merchant; by 2026 vendors in every category sell modules that sit beside an existing stack.

supporting_claims.claim: Platforms with the same features differ in operating model: who runs each part, how the cost moves and what leaving costs.
The market sells commerce platforms in seven categories, and each category puts the integration work in a different place; none removes it.
Platforms are priced mainly on the merchant's sales and payments, so the subscription is the smallest line of the cost.
Between 2023 and 2026 vendors in every category began selling layers that sit beside an existing stack, so a 2026 pitch is a layer to add.
A vendor's numbers and public record can be read: every number has a unit, a date and a definition, and funding, upgrades, price and ownership change in ways a merchant can watch.
A merchant should choose the category by the work its team can carry at its scale stage, which for Kestrel & Pine means keeping its shop platform and adding layers beside it.

role.contribution: Closes the part by connecting the map and the ownership decisions to what a merchant can buy.

additional_patterns.applies_to: tour, wrong: parallel categories and parallel failure modes
scene to place: two proposals posed, then tested once the map exists

flow.rationale: The scene poses three questions the reader cannot yet answer. The categories are named first because every later section uses their names. The reading guide comes before the vendor-by-vendor section because that section is where the reader meets the vendors' numbers; placed after it, the guide arrived when the numbers had already been taken at face value (round 1 of the draft check). Pricing follows the vendors because the price lists were met one by one and the cost-shape row of the trade-off table and the stage table's fee reviews need the pricing models; the trade-offs precede the stages because the stages apply the rule the trade-offs end on. The 2023–2026 record comes after the stages because its reading (vendors now sell what a merchant below the Group stage can absorb) needs the stage judgment, and it stands directly before the test of Kestrel & Pine's proposals because those are two such pitches. The test comes only then, since it uses the categories, the prices, the team rule and the stage. The failure modes could precede the test; they stay last because 'When It Goes Wrong' closes the body in every chapter of the book.

hook.content: Two commerce platforms can offer the same cart, catalog and checkout features while giving a merchant very different work to do: with one the vendor runs the servers and storefront; with another the merchant must operate a separate storefront and manage upgrades.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone comparing two products starts with their feature lists.
bridge.to_topic: The work a platform leaves to the merchant (running, upgrading, paying fees that grow with sales, leaving) is its operating model, and the categories of the market are different operating models.

thesis_statement.text: The category decides where the integration work and the cost land, not whether they exist; pick the category by who you have to carry that work, and read every 2026 pitch as a layer to add, not a reason to move.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Two Pitches in One Week

advances_thesis.how: Shows the operating-model questions (what kind of platform, what it costs in year three, what a move would fix) as questions a merchant is actually asked.

sections.heading: Seven Kinds of Platform
sections.controlling_idea: The market sells the shop platform in seven categories, and each puts the integration work in a different place without removing it.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the product and the categories and states the rule that integration work moves and never disappears.

flow.rationale: The product is defined, then the table of categories, then the four terms the table uses (readers of round 2 could not hold terms defined before the table they belong to), then the rule about the fourth column, which the vendor-by-vendor section illustrates.

transition_in.carries_over: Mara's first question: what kind of platform are we on?
transition_in.introduces: The seven kinds the market sells.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In the market's vocabulary a commerce platform is the product a merchant buys to show products, hold a cart, take the order and the payment and hand the order on, which this book calls the shop platform; in this chapter 'platform' means that product, and 'commerce platform' in the book's sense stays the whole set of systems.
The market sells the product in seven overlapping categories that differ in what is bought, who runs it and where the integration work lands.

evidence.what: Seven categories (hosted SaaS platform, enterprise suite, open source and its forks, composable and headless vendor, ERP-centered commerce, specialist layer, specialist group), each with examples, what you buy, who runs it and where the integration work lands.
evidence.shows: Each category is a different answer to who runs the product and who carries the integration work.
evidence.source: The author's synthesis from vendor pages and filings (2025–2026)

transition_in.carries_over: The product called a platform.
transition_in.introduces: The seven categories in which the market sells it, in one table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four terms in the table need defining: SaaS is software the vendor runs for many customers at once, a suite is one vendor's modules designed to work together, headless separates the storefront from the commerce engine behind an API, and composable means buying commerce as separate services and assembling them.

transition_in.carries_over: The category table.
transition_in.introduces: Four terms in it that need defining.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The fourth column matters most: every category moves the integration work somewhere and none removes it, so the choice is who carries the work, at what price and with what freedom to change.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's 34 integrations exist because it chose a hosted platform and bought specialist layers around it; a suite would have fewer joins and one larger contract, a composable assembly more joins, all its own.
evidence.shows: The same merchant would carry a different amount and kind of integration work in each category.

evidence.what: Figure 2: each category asks the merchant for a different kind of work and joins the specialist layers in a different place.
evidence.shows: The burden changes place from category to category and never reaches zero.

transition_in.carries_over: The table's four columns.
transition_in.introduces: The fourth, where the integration work lands, and the rule that it moves and is never removed.

sections.heading: How to Read a Vendor's Claims
sections.controlling_idea: A vendor's number, and a market-share figure, can be compared only when its unit, date and definition are known.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the reader the test to apply to every number in the vendor-by-vendor section and in any pitch.

transition_in.carries_over: The seven categories and the rule about where the work lands.
transition_in.introduces: What to ask of the vendor numbers the next section is full of, before meeting them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The vendor paragraphs that follow are full of numbers, and no number can be compared across vendors until its unit, its date and its definition are known; the table takes its examples from those paragraphs.

evidence.what: Four kinds of claimed unit (GMV; merchants, customers, brands, users; marketplaces, integrations, apps; surveys, analyst charts and performance claims), each with a dated example and the trap.
evidence.shows: The same word counts different things at different vendors, so a number cannot be compared until its unit, date and definition are known.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Market-share data need the same care, because two true figures can rank the same vendor last and first when they count different populations.

evidence.what: W3Techs (7 November 2026): WooCommerce 47.3% of sites with a detectable e-commerce technology, Shopify 32.5%, Shopware 0.2%; EHI: Shopware first among the 1,000 largest German shops.
evidence.shows: A count of websites and a count of large shops rank the same vendor last and first.

transition_in.carries_over: Vendor numbers and their traps.
transition_in.introduces: Market-share data, which need the same care.

sections.heading: The Seven Kinds, Vendor by Vendor
sections.controlling_idea: The public record of each category's vendors shows who runs the product, how it is priced and where the integration work lands.

advances_thesis.how: Gives each category dated public evidence, read by unit, date and definition, and shows the work moving from category to category.

flow.rationale: One sentence says how each category is read; the categories then follow the rows of the category table, the specialist layers and the group last because they are defined by what surrounds the other five; the Eurostat statistic closes the section because it puts the whole list of webshop vendors in proportion and follows the one vendor paragraph that names an EDI provider.

transition_in.carries_over: The seven categories, and the habit of asking a number's unit, date and definition.
transition_in.introduces: Each category read from its vendors' filings, price lists and announcements.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each of the seven kinds is described below from its vendors' public record.

The hosted platform is the default for a merchant that starts online, and Shopify's filing and price list show its shape: a monthly plan plus fees that move with sales, with most merchants on the cheapest plans and most sales volume from the largest merchants.

evidence.what: Shopify FY2025: GMV $378.4 billion, revenue $11.56 billion; plans from Basic €28 to Plus from €2,100 a month; card rates 1.9% + €0.25 down to 1.4% + €0.25; 2% down to 0.2% on orders paid through another provider; a variable platform fee for larger Plus merchants.
evidence.shows: A hosted platform charges a subscription and, on top of it, fees tied to the merchant's sales.
evidence.source: Shopify Form 10-K (11 February 2026); Shopify pricing page (November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: The promise of a record per category.
transition_in.introduces: The first category, hosted SaaS, through Shopify's filing and price list.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: BigCommerce, now under the parent Commerce.com, assigns plans by the merchant's trailing sales, which is a price on sales under a subscription's name, and its 2026 results report flat revenue and soft demand for replatforming.

evidence.what: Plans assigned by trailing-twelve-month GMV with 0.9% above $33,333 a month on the Scale plan; quarter ended 30 June 2026: revenue $84.5 million, up 0.1%; B2C replatforming 'remains softer than historically'.
evidence.shows: A subscription tier set by sales is GMV pricing; the vendor itself reports that merchants are not moving platforms.
evidence.source: BigCommerce pricing page (November 2026); Commerce.com Q2 2026 results (6 August 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: Shopify's plan-plus-fees pricing.
transition_in.introduces: BigCommerce: plans assigned by sales, and soft replatforming demand.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Lightspeed earns more than twice as much from transactions as from subscriptions and has named growth engines that exclude European online retail, which the author reads, as a labeled inference, as a vendor-risk signal for a Dutch merchant on its e-commerce product.

evidence.what: Strategic review closed 6 February 2025: 'focus on growing retail in North America and hospitality in Europe'; FY2026 transaction-based revenue $815.1 million against subscription revenue $370.7 million; Dutch eCom €68 to €259 a month.
evidence.shows: The revenue mix and the stated strategy are public signals of where a vendor will invest.

evidence.what: Callout 'INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED': Lightspeed has announced no change to its European e-commerce product; the risk reading is the author's.
evidence.shows: Separates the documented fact from the author's reading of it.

transition_in.carries_over: Two listed hosted vendors.
transition_in.introduces: A third, Lightspeed, whose revenue mix and strategy are a risk signal.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Below the listed vendors sit smaller hosted products such as the Dutch CCV Shop, priced at a flat monthly fee and not as a share of sales, and the site builders.

evidence.what: CCV Shop: €36 to €129 a month, 'not a percentage of your sales'.
evidence.shows: Flat pricing exists at the small end of the hosted category.

transition_in.carries_over: Vendors that earn on the merchant's sales.
transition_in.introduces: Small hosted products priced at a flat fee.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Enterprise suites sell to large merchants through implementation partners at negotiated prices, so their public evidence is thin; SAP Commerce Cloud is described here only from its open-source storefront project and one analyst note.

evidence.what: The Spartacus storefront project (accessed November 2026) and an October 2026 analyst note reporting an 'SAP Commerce Cloud, cloud ERP edition' and warning buyers to 'separate products that are available now from forward-looking demonstrations'.
evidence.shows: What can be said about SAP from public sources, and that the author quotes no feature list.

transition_in.carries_over: The hosted category and its public evidence.
transition_in.introduces: Enterprise suites, sold through partners, with thinner evidence; SAP first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Salesforce sells one platform across consumer and business selling, point of sale and order management, now with AI agents connected to it, and publishes no price; that it charges a percentage of sales is industry belief, not a documented fact.

evidence.what: 6 July 2026: 'its biggest Agentforce Commerce release yet', three generally available agents 'natively connected to catalog, inventory, and orders'; pricing page shows 'Contact for pricing' for every edition.
evidence.shows: A suite's selling point is one connected data model; its price is negotiated and not public.
evidence.source: Salesforce press release and pricing page (2026)

transition_in.carries_over: SAP, described from two public sources.
transition_in.introduces: Salesforce: one connected platform and no public price.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adobe Commerce shows one product in three deployment shapes (on-premises, platform-as-a-service, fully managed SaaS), and the middle shape, where the vendor runs the servers and the merchant owns the code, is where deep customization can block every upgrade.

evidence.what: Adobe's information center (updated 21 October 2026) lists Adobe Commerce on-premises, on cloud infrastructure and as a Cloud Service; Adobe Commerce Optimizer 'can work alongside an existing Adobe Commerce or third-party commerce backend'; partner reports place both launches in June 2025.
evidence.shows: Within one vendor the deployment shape, not the feature list, decides who runs hosting and who applies upgrades; the vendor also sells a layer beside another backend.

transition_in.carries_over: Suites with thin public evidence.
transition_in.introduces: Adobe, the clearest public example: one product in three deployment shapes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Open source means the code may be run and changed, not that it is free: hosting, upgrades, security patches and the agency that applies them are the recurring price, as the chain from an Adobe fix to a Mage-OS release to the merchant's own test shows.

evidence.what: Magento Open Source and the community fork Mage-OS: 4.0.0 shipped 30 October 2026; 3.6.0, two weeks earlier, was a security port of an Adobe patch. WooCommerce claims 'more than 4 million stores' and prices hosting at $25 to $350 a month.
evidence.shows: An open-source merchant depends on a chain of parties for every fix and pays for hosting and upgrades.
evidence.source: Mage-OS; WooCommerce pricing (November 2026); Wikipedia on Magento

transition_in.carries_over: Products a vendor runs or co-runs.
transition_in.introduces: Open source: code the merchant runs and upgrades itself, with Magento's open edition and its fork.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopware, the leader among large German shops, shows that an open-source platform can be free for the smallest merchants and priced on sales above that.

evidence.what: 12.5% of the 1,000 largest German B2C shops (EHI 2026), first for the fifth year; Community Edition free; Rise from €600 and Evolve from €2,400 a month 'based on your gross merchandise value'; a paid plan required above €1 million of GMV in a rolling year.
evidence.shows: 'Open source' is free for the smallest merchants and GMV-priced above that.

transition_in.carries_over: Open source and its recurring costs.
transition_in.introduces: Shopware: free at small scale, priced on sales above it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopware is also absorbing payments and integration into the platform, with PayPal as a large shareholder.

evidence.what: PayPal's stake above 40% (October 2025); Shopware Payments on PayPal's infrastructure and Nexus, an orchestration layer positioned as replacing middleware, launched 10 June 2026.
evidence.shows: An open-source platform pulls payments and orchestration inside.
evidence.source: Shopware press releases (2026); Ecommerce News Europe (2025)

transition_in.carries_over: Shopware's pricing.
transition_in.introduces: Shopware absorbing payments and integration, with PayPal as shareholder.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Composable and headless vendors give the merchant a choice of what to replace and leave it responsible for connecting and operating every part it selects.

transition_in.carries_over: Categories built around one core product.
transition_in.introduces: Composable and headless vendors, defined above, and what they leave to the merchant.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: commercetools, the best-known composable vendor, reports large volume, cut staff after missing growth targets, and since 2026 sells layers and standalone modules for stacks that are not composable.

evidence.what: 22 April 2026: '$100B GMV run-rate', more than 600 million orders a year; 26 February 2025: about 10% of staff cut; 21 January 2026: AgenticLift 'on top of your existing commerce solution'; 15 July 2026: cart-and-order engine and product catalog as standalone modules.
evidence.shows: The flagship of composable now sells pieces to add beside an existing platform.

transition_in.carries_over: What composable leaves to the merchant.
transition_in.introduces: commercetools and Saleor.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Saleor shows that API-only vendors price on the merchant's sales too.

evidence.what: Saleor cloud from $1,599 a month up to $200,000 of monthly GMV, 0.8% above (November 2026).
evidence.shows: Pricing on sales is not particular to hosted platforms.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The categories, the price lists and the vendors' 2023–2026 record describe the same three things from different sides: who runs the product, how its price moves with the merchant's sales and who carries the integration work. A move between categories changes the owner of that work and does not remove it, so the question to put to any pitch is what it would fix that an added layer would not.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant that can say who carries the work in each category can refuse a move that would only change the work's owner and price; Kestrel & Pine stays on its shop platform and adds the layers it lacks.
